q: A green precipitate forms when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution. The precipitate dissolves in excess to give a green solution. Which cation is present?
explain: Chromium(III) hydroxide is green and dissolves in excess alkali. Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate that stays, and zinc gives a white precipitate.

q: A pale green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide turns brown at the surface when left in air. What is the explanation?
options: Iron(III) ions are reduced to iron(II) ions by the air.
Iron(II) ions are oxidised to iron(III) ions by oxygen in the air.
Carbon dioxide in the air reacts with the precipitate.
explain: Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺ by oxygen, forming red-brown iron(III) hydroxide on the surface.

q: Which ionic equation represents the formation of the precipitate when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate?
explain: Each Cu²⁺ ion needs two OH⁻ ions to balance the charge, and the hydroxide is insoluble, so (s) is shown.

q: What is the formula of the red-brown precipitate formed when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to aqueous iron(III) chloride?
explain: Fe³⁺ combines with three OH⁻ ions to give iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃. Fe(OH)₂ is the green iron(II) hydroxide.

q: A solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess. With aqueous ammonia it gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
explain: Both Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide, but only the zinc precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia. So the cation is aluminium.

q: A solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess. A flame test gives a brick-red flame. Which cation is present?
explain: A white precipitate insoluble in excess alkali and a brick-red flame are both characteristic of calcium. Barium gives a green flame and aluminium and zinc precipitates dissolve in excess.

q: Why is aqueous sodium hydroxide added to a solution a little at a time and then in excess?
options: to find the volume of alkali needed
to see whether any precipitate that forms dissolves in excess
explain: Whether the precipitate redissolves in excess alkali is part of identifying the cation, for example aluminium and zinc compared with calcium.

q: Which ionic equation represents the release of ammonia when an ammonium salt is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
explain: Ammonium ions give up a hydrogen ion to hydroxide ions, forming ammonia and water. This is the only equation that balances and shows ammonia escaping as a gas.

q: Excess aqueous ammonia is added to a solution of zinc sulfate. What is seen?
options: A white precipitate forms and does not dissolve.
A blue precipitate forms and dissolves to give a dark blue solution.
A white precipitate forms and then dissolves to give a colourless solution.
explain: Zinc hydroxide is a white precipitate that dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution.

q: Which test is used to identify hydrogen?
options: A lighted splint makes a squeaky pop.
Damp red litmus paper turns blue.
explain: Hydrogen burns explosively with oxygen, giving a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

q: Which test and result identify oxygen?
options: A lighted splint makes a squeaky pop.
explain: Oxygen supports combustion, so a glowing splint bursts into flame.

q: Which gas turns limewater milky?
explain: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which makes the limewater milky.

q: A gas turns damp blue litmus paper red and then bleaches it white. Which gas is it?
explain: Chlorine forms an acidic solution in the damp paper, which turns the litmus red, and then bleaches it.

q: A gas turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which gas is it?
explain: Ammonia is the common alkaline gas. It dissolves in the water on the paper to form an alkaline solution.

q: Which gas turns acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless?
explain: Sulfur dioxide is a reducing agent and reduces the purple manganate(VII) ions to colourless Mn²⁺ ions.

q: Which row correctly gives a gas, its test and the positive result?
explain: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint, carbon dioxide turns limewater milky and chlorine bleaches damp litmus.

q: A white precipitate forms when carbon dioxide is bubbled into limewater. What is the precipitate?
explain: Limewater is aqueous calcium hydroxide. It reacts with carbon dioxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

q: A green solid is heated and turns black. The gas produced turns limewater milky. Which solid was heated?
explain: Copper(II) carbonate is green. It decomposes to black copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

q: A colourless gas does not change the colour of acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) but turns limewater milky. Which gas is it?
explain: Both sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide can give a milky limewater, but only sulfur dioxide decolourises acidified manganate(VII). The gas is therefore carbon dioxide.

q: Why must the litmus paper be damp when testing for ammonia?
options: Water cools the ammonia so it can be detected.
Water acts as a catalyst for the colour change.
Water removes carbon dioxide from the gas.
Ammonia dissolves in the water to form an alkaline solution that changes the colour of the litmus.
explain: Dry ammonia gas does not change the colour of litmus. It must dissolve in water on the paper to form alkaline hydroxide ions.

q: Which cation gives a red flame in a flame test?
explain: Lithium compounds give a red flame. Potassium is lilac, sodium is yellow and barium is light green.

q: Which colour does a sodium compound give in a flame test?
explain: Sodium ions give an intense yellow flame.

q: A compound burns in a flame test with a lilac flame. Which cation is present?
explain: Potassium compounds give a lilac flame. Lithium gives red, sodium yellow and copper(II) blue-green.

q: Which cation gives an orange-red flame in a flame test?
explain: Calcium compounds give an orange-red (brick-red) flame. Barium gives a light green flame and copper(II) gives a blue-green flame.

q: Which cation gives a light green flame in a flame test?
explain: Barium compounds give a light green flame.

q: A flame test gives a blue-green flame. Which cation is present?
explain: Copper(II) compounds give a blue-green flame.

q: Which row correctly gives the flame colour for the cation?
explain: Copper(II) is blue-green. Lithium is red, potassium is lilac and sodium is yellow.

q: A white solid gives a lilac flame in a flame test. Its aqueous solution gives a white precipitate with acidified aqueous silver nitrate. What is the solid?
explain: The lilac flame shows potassium, and a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate shows chloride. Iodide would give a yellow precipitate.

q: Why is the wire for a flame test cleaned with dilute hydrochloric acid and heated before use?
options: to remove traces of other substances that could colour the flame
to give the flame a green colour
explain: Contamination on the wire, especially sodium, would give flame colours that mask the colour of the sample being tested.

q: A solid dissolves in water to form a colourless solution. A flame test gives a lilac flame. Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives no precipitate. After acidifying with dilute nitric acid, aqueous barium nitrate gives a white precipitate. What is the solid?
explain: Lilac means potassium. The precipitate with acidified barium nitrate means sulfate. A calcium salt would have given a precipitate with sodium hydroxide.
